sources.name: Hamel Husain & Shreya Shankar — Why AI evals are the hottest new skill

note: This complements the Hamel/Shreya video already in the corpus, which covers the error-analysis PROCESS (open/axial coding, benevolent dictator). This deck covers the specific FRAMEWORKS and METRICS — the vocabulary an interviewer expects you to name.

cards.back: Whether every claim in the generated answer is actually supported by the retrieved context — computed by decomposing the answer into individual claims, then checking each against the context for entailment. Catches hallucination even when the answer sounds fluent.

Whether the answer actually addresses the question asked — computed by generating several synthetic questions the answer would answer, then measuring embedding similarity to the original question. Low relevancy means the answer is accurate but off-topic or evasive.

cards.front: Why is "context precision" alone not enough to judge a RAG system?
cards.back: You can have perfectly relevant retrieved chunks (high precision) but still miss chunks that were needed (low recall) — an answer built on relevant-but-incomplete context. You need both dimensions, broken down by failure type, not one composite score.

cards.front: What's the core architectural difference between DeepEval and Promptfoo?
cards.back: DeepEval is Python/pytest-native — evals run as unit tests and fail your CI build on a metric threshold breach. Promptfoo is a config-driven (YAML), language-agnostic CLI built for side-by-side prompt/model comparison and has a much stronger red-teaming/security-scanning engine (40+ attack types).

cards.front: Why do mature eval stacks run both DeepEval and Promptfoo instead of picking one?
cards.back: They answer different questions: Promptfoo answers "can an attacker break this" (jailbreaks, injection, excessive agency); DeepEval answers "does this meet our quality bar" (faithfulness, hallucination, relevancy). Different failure modes, different tools, both run as CI gates before deploy.

cards.front: In an LLM-as-judge setup, why should the judge always output binary pass/fail rather than a 1-5 score?
cards.back: 1-5 scores collapse into noise — humans and models disagree on what a "3" means, and the score doesn't map to an action. Binary forces a decision and can be directly validated against human labels with a confusion matrix.

cards.front: Why must you validate an LLM judge against human labels before trusting it in production?
cards.back: A judge can silently be biased — e.g., always saying "pass" — and still show high raw agreement if real failures are rare. A confusion matrix breaks that down cell by cell so you see exactly where the judge is wrong, not just an aggregate percentage.

cards.front: What's the difference between a "unit eval" and a "regression eval"?
cards.back: Unit eval tests a single LLM call/component in isolation before deploy, like a unit test. Regression eval runs continuously against production traffic or a fixed dataset to catch silent drift — a model or prompt change degrading quality without an obvious error.

A metric that uses an LLM with chain-of-thought reasoning to score outputs against a custom rubric you define in natural language — more flexible than fixed metrics like BLEU/ROUGE, but still needs validation against human judgment like any LLM-judge.

cards.front: Why is evals now a core product-building skill instead of a QA afterthought?
cards.back: You can't productively iterate on a model or prompt without a way to measure whether a change helped — evals are the feedback loop, not a compliance checkbox. Teams that skip them end up debugging by vibes.
